drafts.title: Colorado: EV home backup with no utility approval
drafts.angle: Your truck can keep the lights on, and Colorado just cut the red tape. Local, independence, money. Do not claim his Model Y does this.
bullets: Colorado PUC approved a settlement Oct 22, 2026 (Ford, Xcel Energy, Black Hills Colorado Electric).
EVs set up as backup-only (power to the house only when it's cut off from the grid) are not interconnection resources: no application, no utility approval.
Simple optional notification (name, address, local permit); no penalty for skipping it.
Systems that push power while still grid-connected still follow interconnection rules. Colorado joins Michigan, Maryland and California.
drafts.body: $0 in utility paperwork. Colorado now says an EV used only as home backup, when the grid's down, doesn't need interconnection approval. My last outage lasted {how long my power was out}. Would you use your truck or car to keep the lights on?
drafts.framework_body:
No application. No utility approval.

Colorado's PUC just signed off on a deal with Ford, Xcel and Black Hills. If your EV only powers your house when the grid is down, it's not treated like a power plant anymore. A simple optional notice is it.

If you want to send power back while still on the grid, that's still the old rules. Fair enough.

My last outage lasted {how long my power was out}. I've got Enphase solar on the roof and {what my solar does in an outage}.

A truck in the driveway that keeps the fridge and furnace running is real independence. Michigan, Maryland and California already did this. Glad Colorado's on the list.

Would you use your truck or car to keep the lights on?
drafts.ocr_why: Local Colorado independence story with a clear rule change and an easy yes/no question.
drafts.pixel: Standing by your panel or solar gateway: "Colorado just made this easier. Here's what I'd want in an outage."
drafts.premium_target: Verified F-150 Lightning / Ford EV owner account, or a Colorado energy reporter covering the PUC decision.
